Engineers or Veterinarians of Voat, What Should I Know About Your Career Before Pursuing it?
Engineering probably varies depending on the type. What type do you want to go into?
I was thinking either mechanical or electrical, which seems to be what most recommend.

What field of engineering? I would strongly advise doing a LOT of research into not only the "day of the life" of an engineer, but where you would be working. I have an engineering degree in a field that I love, but I hated the location choices for a job, so I no longer work in the industry. Also find out what the education levels are for various jobs. I would have done my master's or doctorate in the field because the jobs for bachelor's degrees were so mundane and boring, but a lot of people won't find that out until getting a job and realizing they hate it.

Also I have a few friends who are veterinarians. The worst part for them is dealing with people who just don't care about their dogs anymore and will even just request you to put down a dog because they can't afford care or they are too lazy/broke to go through with a lifesaving procedure for the dog. Emergency vets don't have to deal with people quite as much as general practice, but if you do a more niche area like zoo or wildlife, you don't have to deal with crazy pet owners at all. However, it is tougher to get into and the work can be limited.

I know there are stupid people who will ask me to put down their pet, but if I could save just a few then it would be worth it to me. My problem is trying to justify a lower wage with 4 extra years of schooling. I'm not even sure it's possible to pay back vet school on their wage.

However, I also find engineering and physics particularly interesting. I love understanding how the world works and being able to figure out things most can't even comprehend.

Yes you will be paying off student loans for many, many, many years as a vet. Vets end up with six figures of student loans with no end in sight. If you can do a specialty, you will be slightly better off, but ultimately, if you want a paycheck, go for engineering. Alternatively, do human medical school if you still want to be in the medical field but with a paycheck and find a specialty there.

Engineering covers just about anything. I was especially interested in physics and engineering, so I did nuclear engineering, which was a pretty good mix of the two fields. However, that is also a field I'm hesitant to recommend to others because the work locations are all very rural or in the country because of the land space required for power plants or labs. But if you don't mind living in a small town or more rural area, getting your doctorate in the field and working in a national lab might be a good option. A friend of mine works at Lawrence Livermore as a nuclear engineer; some of the projects there are plutonium research, particle and accelerator physics, and nuclear physics. If you are truly wanting to make engineering work, I would recommend picking the job that you want and figuring out what engineering degree and level of education is needed to make it work. I went into the program just because I liked it without an end goal besides getting my bachelor's, and by the time that I figured out the only job I could get with a bachelor's was a shitty one, I was already pretty disillusioned and burned out with the program itself and moved to another field. Don't do what I did and pick a major just because you like the subject matter; really do research into the sort of jobs that the degree will get you and figure out early on if that's something you want.

If you are going to go into engineering, expect that you will need a MS to get an interesting job. Occasionally engineers will find interesting jobs with a BS, but not often. Either way, expect to travel a lot in your first 10 years and work weeks longer than 50 hours are likely. The pay is pretty good though.
What kinds of jobs can you not get unless you get an MS? I was told by most engineers that the only difference is that you need someone with an MS to approve your designs.

For example, in structural engineering if you have a BS you will be working on designs that are very cookie-cutter in nature. Like a standard overpass bridge over a 2-lane highway, or a Home Depot building. With a MS you are much more likely to work on one-off designs that likely have some interesting features and challenges.

This may not be exactly the case in all fields, but typically the more interesting stuff is more difficult and goes to the more educated/experienced.

Edit: Also, in structural engineering the companies that do the interesting projects, like SOM, pretty much only hire MS and PhD grads for this reason.

I am an Engineer that works for R&D at a DoD research lab.

I can tell you that there are almost no absolutes in the engineering career field. Would you believe that as an civilian Engineer your day job could be riding the backseat of a F/A-18 hornet with the test pilot? You could also end up at a desk pushing buttons or just managing people. Some people say you work long hours and there will be the same amount of people that get 3 hours a week PAID to go exercise and only work 40 hour weeks. Some engineers travel a lot and others never travel.

What you should know about being an Engineer is that the jobs available are so diverse you can pretty much find what you want if you are willing to relocate and have the credentials.

One thing that could give you an edge is diversity. So for example a Mechanical Engineer that can code in C++/Python or anything else or a Electrical Engineer that can weld and run a lathe. That will set you apart from the normal pool and might get you more unique jobs.

One tidbit I can give that may not be specifically about the engineering career field but is relavant to you is this:

This is the Federal Website for Jobs:: https://www.usajobs.gov/

Everyone ( Navy, Army, Airforce, NASA, etc) has to list their jobs there AND their summer internships! If you do decide to go the path of Engineering I would recommend keeping an eye on that webpage from Feb-Jun to see if any great internship opportunities pop up. They will be PAID internships and you should be able to make enough to have room and board as well.
